secondaryCondition: Osteomalacia (defective bone mineralization, renal osteodystrophy spectrum) in a veteran with service-connected chronic kidney disease
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5014 (osteomalacia, residuals of) — evaluated as degenerative arthritis based on limitation of motion of affected parts under the note to DCs 5013 through 5024; because osteomalacia often presents with bone pain, proximal myopathy, and fractures rather than joint limitation, a clinically justified analogous evaluation under §§ 4.20 and 4.27 may be required, and residual fractures are separately rated under the fracture codes. Qualified-human rating review required
primaryCondition: Service-connected chronic kidney disease (chronic renal failure) with documented reduction in glomerular filtration rate and laboratory evidence of disordered mineral metabolism
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.115b, DC 7530 (chronic renal disease requiring regular dialysis) and DC 7502 (nephritis, chronic), each rated as renal dysfunction under the criteria of § 4.115a; DC 7537 (interstitial nephritis, including disorders of calcium metabolism) is the alternative code where that is the documented renal pathology. Note that the schedule provides no free-standing chronic-kidney-disease code, so the renal dysfunction evaluation in § 4.115a supplies the rating level
etiologicalMechanism: Renal mineral-metabolism sequence: as glomerular filtration falls in service-connected chronic kidney disease, phosphate retention and reduced renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation of vitamin D produce hypocalcemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism. The resulting chronic parathyroid hormone excess drives high bone turnover (osteitis fibrosa), while the deficiency of active vitamin D and the accumulation of uremic toxins impair osteoblast-mediated deposition of mineral into osteoid, so newly formed bone matrix remains unmineralized — the histologic definition of osteomalacia. In dialysis-treated and advanced disease, additional contributors include aluminum or iron accumulation and hypophosphatemia after aggressive phosphate control, and the mixed uremic osteodystrophy picture in which osteomalacia coexists with hyperparathyroid bone disease. Pazianas and Miller (PMID 33774081) situate osteoporosis, osteomalacia, and the forms of renal osteodystrophy within the single spectrum of chronic kidney disease-mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD), which is the framing that makes an osteomalacia claim in kidney disease medically coherent. Hou et al. (PMID 30298663) review mineral bone disorders in chronic kidney disease and define CKD-MBD as abnormal metabolism of calcium, phosphorus, parathyroid hormone, or vitamin D together with abnormalities in bone turnover, mineralization, volume, linear growth, or strength — the mineralization-abnormality limb of that definition being the osteomalacia mechanism asserted here. Patel and Hashmi (PMID 32809577) describe the CKD-MBD syndrome as encompassing disordered calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone, vitamin D, and fibroblast growth factor-23 metabolism leading to altered bone morphology (renal osteodystrophy) and vascular calcification. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) direct-causation theory — the service-connected renal failure is asserted to have produced a distinct metabolic bone disease, osteomalacia, and not merely to have aggravated an existing skeletal disorder. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would be the correct theory only where the record documents pre-existing osteomalacia or osteoporosis from another cause (for example, malabsorption, prior gastric surgery, or anticonvulsant therapy) and the claim is that the renal disease measurably worsened that baseline mineralization defect, in which case the renal-attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of the pre-existing bone disease and § 3.310(b) governs. Chronology and the individual analysis under § 3.310(a) or (b) require a documented sequence in which the decline in renal function precedes the metabolic bone disease, and they require objective evidence of osteomalacia rather than of osteoporosis alone: elevated alkaline phosphatase, low or low-normal serum phosphate, appropriate parathyroid hormone levels, and ideally bone biopsy showing increased osteoid volume and mineralization lag time, or imaging and dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry findings interpreted with the knowledge that bone mineral density is unreliable in advanced kidney disease. Only with that evidence can an examiner state that the osteomalacia is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected chronic kidney disease — a conclusion requiring documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102, not a transfer of the population association to the individual claimant. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include vitamin D deficiency from inadequate sun exposure or diet, malabsorption from celiac disease, bariatric surgery, or pancreatic insufficiency, anticonvulsant and tenofovir therapy, hypophosphatemic and other inherited phosphate-wasting disorders, primary hyperparathyroidism, liver disease, prior gastrectomy, and coexisting age-related or glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, which is a separate disease and should not be relabeled as osteomalacia. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating discipline under § 4.14: osteomalacia cannot be compensated simultaneously under DC 5014 and again as the same limitation of motion or fracture through another code, and the note to DCs 5013 through 5024 requires a single evaluation as degenerative arthritis on limitation of motion where that is the predominant disability picture.

medicalEvidence.title: Osteoporosis and Chronic Kidney Disease-Mineral and Bone Disorder (CKD-MBD): Back to Basics
medicalEvidence.summary: Review article stating that, on the basis of bone histology, osteoporosis is only one part of a spectrum of skeletal complications that includes osteomalacia and the various forms of renal osteodystrophy of chronic kidney disease-mineral and bone disorder — the framing evidence that osteomalacia is a kidney-disease skeletal complication.

medicalEvidence.title: Mineral bone disorders in chronic kidney disease
medicalEvidence.authors: Yi-Chou Hou; Chien-Lin Lu; Kuo-Cheng Lu
medicalEvidence.summary: Review documenting that as glomerular filtration loss aggravates, disturbed mineral metabolism worsens bone microstructure and remodeling in what is termed CKD-mineral bone disease, characterized by abnormal calcium, phosphorus, parathyroid hormone, or vitamin D metabolism and by abnormalities in bone turnover, mineralization, volume, linear growth, or strength — the mineralization-defect mechanism.

medicalEvidence.title: Chronic Kidney Disease-Mineral Bone Disorder (CKD-MBD)
medicalEvidence.summary: StatPearls review of the CKD-MBD syndrome, tracing the term to the recognition that disorders of calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone, vitamin D, and fibroblast growth factor-23 metabolism produce altered bone morphology (renal osteodystrophy) and vascular calcification in kidney disease — corroborating the mineral-metabolism derangement asserted in this row.

secondaryCondition: Vocal cord paralysis (recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy with hoarseness or aphonia) following thyroidectomy performed for service-connected thyroid enlargement
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.97, DC 6516 (laryngitis, chronic): 30 percent for hoarseness with thickening or nodules of cords, polyps, submucous infiltration, or pre-malignant changes on biopsy; 10 percent for hoarseness with inflammation of cords or mucous membrane. Where the injury is complete, DC 6519 (aphonia, complete organic) pays 100 percent for constant inability to communicate by speech and 60 percent for constant inability to speak above a whisper, and its note directs that incomplete aphonia be evaluated as laryngitis, chronic (DC 6516). DC 6520 (larynx, stenosis of, including residuals of laryngeal trauma) may apply where stenosis or flow-volume-loop-confirmed upper airway obstruction follows. Qualified-human rating review required
primaryCondition: Service-connected nontoxic thyroid enlargement (goiter) severe enough to require thyroidectomy
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.119, DC 7902 (thyroid enlargement, nontoxic), with Note (1) requiring symptoms due to pressure on adjacent organs such as the trachea, larynx, or esophagus to be evaluated under the appropriate diagnostic code within the appropriate body system and Note (2) permitting separate evaluation of neck disfigurement under DC 7800
etiologicalMechanism: Surgical-nerve-injury sequence: the recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove and passes in intimate proximity to the thyroid gland's inferior pole before entering the larynx, where it supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid. Thyroidectomy performed to treat service-connected goiter therefore places the nerve at direct risk: traction, thermal spread from electrocautery, ligature entrapment, or transection produces neurapraxia or axonal loss, and the resulting loss of adductor and abductor innervation leaves the vocal fold immobile in a paramedian or intermediate position with hoarseness, breathy dysphonia, impaired cough, and — when the insult is bilateral or severe — inspiratory stridor or aphonia. Jeannon et al. (PMID 19335706), a systematic review of reported incidence after thyroid surgery, found an average temporary recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy rate of 9.8 percent and a permanent palsy rate of 2.3 percent, with rates varying by extent of surgery and case mix. Hayward et al. (PMID 22989215) reviewed recurrent laryngeal nerve injury in thyroid surgery and reported permanent palsy in 0.3 to 3 percent of cases with transient palsies in 5 to 8 percent, emphasizing identification of high-risk patients. Alkaf et al. (PMID 41047809) retrospectively assessed vocal cord palsy after thyroidectomy and reported an overall permanent vocal cord palsy incidence of approximately 2.9 percent with left and right cord involvement of 1 percent and 1.9 percent respectively, and analyzed associated risk factors. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) proximate-causation theory. The theory is that a disability resulting from treatment of a service-connected condition is itself proximately due to that service-connected condition, so the service-connected goiter that necessitated the thyroidectomy is the legal and medical predicate for a nerve injury caused by the operation undertaken to treat it; the theory is not that the goiter mechanically paralyzed the cord, unless compressive or retrosternal goiter with documented preoperative cord palsy is separately shown. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would govern only where the record shows pre-existing vocal cord dysfunction (for example, from a prior thyroid or cervical spine operation, intubation trauma, or idiopathic palsy) and the claim is that the goiter-directed surgery worsened a baseline deficit, in which case the surgical increment must be separated from the natural progression of the pre-existing palsy and § 3.310(b) applies. Chronology and the individual analysis under § 3.310(a) or (b) require documentation that the goiter and its surgical indication precede the onset of dysphonia, that the surgery was actually performed for the service-connected goiter, and that the postoperative course records hoarseness or dysphonia with laryngoscopic confirmation of vocal fold immobility; where the record lacks a preoperative laryngoscopy, the examiner must address whether the palsy was pre-existing. With that evidence an examiner can state that the vocal cord paralysis is at least as likely as not caused by the thyroidectomy performed for the service-connected thyroid enlargement — a conclusion requiring documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include anesthetic or intubation-related cord trauma, pre-existing idiopathic or compressive palsy, superior laryngeal nerve injury (a different nerve with a different functional deficit), viral neuritis, stroke or other central causes, laryngeal malignancy, prior neck surgery or radiation, and coincidental presbylaryngis; the rates published in the cited series are population incidences and do not establish the cause in a given veteran. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating discipline under § 4.14: the same dysphonia and airway findings may not be rated simultaneously under DC 6516 and DC 6519, and where a laryngectomy or partial laryngectomy has been performed, the schedule requires residuals to be rated under DC 6516, DC 6519, or DC 6520 rather than duplicated.

medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review of the reported incidence of recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy after thyroid surgery, finding an average temporary palsy rate of 9.8 percent and a permanent palsy rate of 2.3 percent, with variation by extent of surgery — the primary incidence evidence for the surgical-injury pathway.

medicalEvidence.title: Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury in thyroid surgery: a review
medicalEvidence.authors: Nathan James Hayward; Simon Grodski; Meei Yeung; William R Johnson; Jonathan Serpell
medicalEvidence.summary: Review of recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy in thyroid surgery reporting permanent palsy in 0.3 to 3 percent of cases and transient palsies in 5 to 8 percent, with attention to high-risk patients and intraoperative nerve identification — corroborating the mechanism and magnitude of the surgical risk.

medicalEvidence.authors: Hussein Alkaf; Sarah Abuduruk; Sara Bayounos; Sherif Kamel Abdelmonim; Jabir Alharbi; Mohammad Ali Alessa; Haddad Alkaff; Ameen Alherabid
medicalEvidence.summary: Retrospective cohort assessing permanent vocal cord palsy after thyroidectomy, reporting overall permanent vocal cord palsy in about 2.9 percent of cases with laterality data and risk-factor analysis — a contemporary incidence estimate for the specific outcome asserted here.

secondaryCondition: Tendinopathy (fluoroquinolone-associated tendinitis, tendinosis, or tendon rupture) in a veteran treated with a fluoroquinolone for service-connected chronic prostatitis
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.71a, DC 5024 (tenosynovitis, tendinitis, tendinosis or tendinopathy) — evaluated as degenerative arthritis based on limitation of motion of affected parts under the note to DCs 5013 through 5024, with the ankle and foot joint codes (for example DC 5271, ankle limited motion) supplying the limitation-of-motion evaluation where the Achilles tendon is involved. Qualified-human rating review required; where the schedule's analogue produces an inappropriately low result for a documented tendon rupture with functional loss, the analogous-rating rule of §§ 4.20 and 4.27 must be considered
primaryCondition: Service-connected chronic prostatitis (chronic bacterial prostatitis) for which systemic fluoroquinolone therapy was prescribed
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.115b, DC 7525 (prostatitis, urethritis, epididymitis, orchitis (unilateral or bilateral), chronic only) — rated as urinary tract infection, with tubercular infections rated under §§ 4.88b or 4.89
etiologicalMechanism: Pharmacological iatrogenic sequence: fluoroquinolones chelate divalent cations and inhibit tenocyte proliferation and collagen synthesis, induce matrix metalloproteinase activity and extracellular-matrix degradation, generate reactive oxygen species and mitochondrial toxicity in tenocytes, and impair tendon stem-cell differentiation, so the tendon loses tensile strength and becomes prone to microtearing. Because the Achilles tendon is subject to the highest repetitive tensile loads in the body and has a relatively poor vascular supply in its mid-substance, it is the archetypal site, and the risk rises with age, with corticosteroid co-administration, with renal impairment, and with longer or repeated courses — which is directly relevant to chronic prostatitis, where fluoroquinolones are used in prolonged regimens. Alves et al. (PMID 31270563), a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies, quantified the elevated risk of tendon injury associated with fluoroquinolone exposure, establishing the association at pooled-analytic strength rather than as anecdote. Shu et al. (PMID 36147351) analyzed the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System for 2016 to 2021 and found that a majority of reported fluoroquinolone-associated suspected tendinitis and tendon rupture cases resulted in serious outcomes, with disproportionality signals for ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, and moxifloxacin. Duman et al. (PMID 40005998) review fluoroquinolone-mediated tendinopathy and tendon rupture and note that although several effects on tendon tissue are identified — changes in gene expression, metabolism, and function of tendon-resident cells — the exact molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood, which is a limitation the individual nexus opinion must disclose rather than overstate. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) proximate-causation theory pleaded as a medication side effect, in which a disability caused by treatment of a service-connected condition is itself service-connected because the treatment was undertaken for the service-connected chronic prostatitis. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would govern only where the record shows pre-existing tendon disease or degenerative tendinopathy and the claim is that the antibiotic exposure worsened a baseline tendon condition, in which case the drug-attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of that baseline tendinopathy and § 3.310(b) applies. Chronology is the decisive element and the corresponding § 3.310(a) or (b) analysis requires: an actual prescription record identifying the fluoroquinolone, dose, and dates; onset of tendon pain during or within the recognized post-exposure window after the course; imaging or examination findings of tendinopathy or rupture; and identification of the prescriber's indication as the service-connected chronic prostatitis. Only then can an examiner state that the tendinopathy is at least as likely as not caused by the fluoroquinolone therapy — a conclusion requiring documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include degenerative Achilles tendinopathy, prior ankle trauma or surgery, systemic corticosteroid use (an independent and synergistic risk factor), diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, hyperlipidemia and statin therapy, inflammatory arthropathy and enthesitis, gout, and repetitive occupational loading; because the reporting systems cited capture suspected associations rather than adjudicated causes, none of them converts into an individual probability. No individual probability is asserted here. No intentional rechallenge, unsupervised discontinuation of a prescribed antibiotic, or patient-specific prescribing recommendation is made. Rating discipline under § 4.14: the same tendon limitation of motion and pain may not be compensated twice, and where the affected joint also carries a separate service-connected arthritic or traumatic rating, the schedule's note to DCs 5013 through 5024 requires a single evaluation for the limitation of motion.

medicalEvidence.title: Fluoroquinolones and the risk of tendon injury: a systematic review and meta-analysis
medicalEvidence.authors: Carlos Alves; Diogo Mendes; Francisco Batel Marques
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies quantifying the risk of tendon injury associated with fluoroquinolone exposure, noting that tendinopathy is a recognized adverse reaction and providing pooled-analytic support for the drug-to-tendon pathway.

medicalEvidence.title: Fluoroquinolone-associated suspected tendonitis and tendon rupture: A pharmacovigilance analysis from 2016 to 2021 based on the FAERS database
medicalEvidence.authors: Yamin Shu; Qilin Zhang; Xucheng He; Yanxin Liu; Pan Wu; Li Chen
medicalEvidence.summary: Pharmacovigilance disproportionality analysis of the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System finding signals for tendonitis and tendon rupture with ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, and moxifloxacin and reporting that most reported cases resulted in serious outcomes — the contemporary safety-signal evidence.

medicalEvidence.title: Fluoroquinolone-Mediated Tendinopathy and Tendon Rupture
medicalEvidence.authors: Ezgi Duman; Sigrid Müller-Deubert; Girish Pattappa; Ioannis Stratos; Stephan A Sieber; Hauke Clausen-Schaumann; Victoria Sarafian; Chisa Shukunami; Maximilian Rudert; Denitsa Docheva
medicalEvidence.summary: Review of fluoroquinolone-mediated tendinopathy and tendon rupture describing the drug class's potential to trigger severe side effects including tendinopathy and tendon rupture and detailing effects on tendon-resident cell gene expression, metabolism, and function, while candidly recording that the exact molecular mechanisms remain unclear — the mechanistic source together with its stated uncertainty.

secondaryCondition: Raynaud's syndrome (secondary Raynaud's phenomenon with digital vasospasm, and its digital ulcer and auto-amputation sequelae) in a veteran with service-connected systemic sclerosis
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.104, DC 7117 (Raynaud's syndrome (also known as secondary Raynaud's phenomenon or secondary Raynaud's)): 100 percent with two or more digital ulcers plus auto-amputation of one or more digits and a history of characteristic attacks; 60 percent with two or more digital ulcers and history of characteristic attacks; 40 percent for characteristic attacks occurring at least daily; 20 percent for attacks four to six times a week; 10 percent for attacks one to three times a week; with the note that these evaluations are for Raynaud's syndrome as a whole regardless of the number of extremities involved. DC 7124 governs primary Raynaud's disease only and must not be used here. Qualified-human rating review required
primaryCondition: Service-connected systemic sclerosis (scleroderma), with documented cutaneous or visceral involvement
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.118, DC 7821 (cutaneous manifestations of collagen-vascular diseases not listed elsewhere (including scleroderma, calcinosis cutis, subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus, and dermatomyositis)) — evaluated under the General Rating Formula for the Skin; visceral involvement is separately rated in the affected body system, for example esophageal disease under § 4.114
etiologicalMechanism: Microvascular and fibrotic vascular sequence: in service-connected systemic sclerosis, endothelial injury with intimal proliferation and progressive obliterative vasculopathy narrows the digital arteries and arterioles, while platelet activation, increased endothelin-1 and reduced nitric oxide and prostacyclin signaling shift the digital vascular bed toward vasoconstriction and impaired vasodilation. The consequence is an exaggerated, reversible digital vasospasm in response to cold or emotional stress — Raynaud's phenomenon — which in systemic sclerosis is not a benign primary disorder but a marker and driver of progressive digital ischemia; when the vasospasm and fixed structural narrowing coexist, persistent hypoperfusion produces digital pitting scars, ischemic ulcers, and auto-amputation of fingertips. Hughes et al. (PMID 32099191) state that Raynaud phenomenon occurs in virtually all patients with systemic sclerosis and is often the earliest clinical manifestation, and that it is caused by impaired digital perfusion requiring careful assessment. Sunderkötter and Riemekasten (PMID 16987831) describe Raynaud's phenomenon in systemic sclerosis as an initial event in the pathophysiological cascade leading to sclerosis, characterized by recurrent reversible spasms of small arterioles and digital arteries triggered by cold and emotional stress and producing the characteristic sudden pallor of the digits. Maciejewska et al. (PMID 35566614) review Raynaud's phenomenon with a focus on systemic sclerosis and state that systemic sclerosis is one of the most frequent causes of secondary Raynaud's phenomenon and that its appearance may occur long before other signs and symptoms, emphasizing the treatment distinction between primary and secondary forms. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) direct-causation theory — the service-connected systemic sclerosis is asserted to have produced a separate, separately rated vascular condition, secondary Raynaud's phenomenon, with its own diagnostic code at DC 7117 rather than being folded into the skin or musculoskeletal evaluation of the scleroderma itself. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; an aggravation theory would be required only where the record shows pre-existing primary Raynaud's disease (DC 7124) or cold-injury-related vasospasm and the claim is that the systemic sclerosis measurably worsened a baseline vasospastic disorder, in which case the attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of the primary disease and § 3.310(b) governs. Chronology and the individual analysis under § 3.310(a) or (b) require documented systemic sclerosis with American College of Rheumatology or EULAR classification features (for example, sclerodactyly, specific autoantibodies, nailfold capillary abnormalities, or internal-organ involvement), a clinical description of characteristic attacks meeting the DC 7117 note definition — sequential digital color change lasting minutes to hours, precipitated by cold or emotional stress — and a temporal relationship in which the vasospastic attacks begin with or after disease onset. Where digital ulcers or auto-amputation are asserted for the 60 or 100 percent tiers, the ulcer history and imaging or photographic documentation must be of record. Only then can an examiner state that the Raynaud's syndrome is at least as likely as not caused by the service-connected systemic sclerosis — a conclusion requiring documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include primary Raynaud's disease (which is the schedule's separate DC 7124 entity), cold-injury residuals under DC 7122 (whose note directs separate evaluation of Raynaud's syndrome unless those findings already support an evaluation there), cigarette smoking and other vasoconstrictor exposure, beta-blocker, ergotamine, or stimulant medication, hypothyroidism, carpal tunnel syndrome and thoracic outlet syndrome, vibration-tool exposure, cryoglobulinemia, and other connective tissue diseases such as mixed connective tissue disease or systemic lupus erythematosus, which are distinct service-connected or non-service-connected identities and must not be merged with systemic sclerosis. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating discipline under § 4.14: DC 7117 evaluations are for Raynaud's syndrome as a whole, so the same digital attacks, ulcers, or amputations may not be compensated a second time under the cold-injury code or as residuals of the scleroderma skin evaluation, and separate amputation ratings follow only the amputation rule and the schedule's own provisions.

medicalEvidence.title: Raynaud phenomenon and digital ulcers in systemic sclerosis
medicalEvidence.authors: Michael Hughes; Yannick Allanore; Lorinda Chung; John D Pauling; Christopher P Denton; Marco Matucci-Cerinic
medicalEvidence.summary: Review stating that Raynaud phenomenon occurs in virtually all patients with systemic sclerosis and is often the earliest clinical manifestation, that it results from impaired digital perfusion, and that careful assessment is required — the primary evidence that the vasospastic disorder is a manifestation of the sclerosis rather than an unrelated condition.

medicalEvidence.title: Pathophysiology and clinical consequences of Raynaud's phenomenon related to systemic sclerosis
medicalEvidence.summary: Article describing Raynaud's phenomenon as an initial event in the pathophysiological cascade leading to sclerosis in systemic sclerosis, characterized by recurrent reversible spasms of small arterioles and digital arteries triggered by cold and emotional stress — the mechanistic account of the vascular pathway asserted in this row.

medicalEvidence.authors: Magdalena Maciejewska; Mariusz Sikora; Cezary Maciejewski; Rosanna Alda-Malicka; Joanna Czuwara; Lidia Rudnicka
medicalEvidence.summary: Review reporting that systemic sclerosis is one of the most frequent causes of secondary Raynaud's phenomenon, that its appearance may occur long before other signs and symptoms, and that treatment differs by underlying cause — the classification evidence distinguishing secondary from primary Raynaud's.

secondaryCondition: Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (drug-induced, with annular photosensitive lesions and Ro/SS-A autoantibodies) in a veteran receiving hydrochlorothiazide for service-connected hypertension
secondaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.118, DC 7821 (cutaneous manifestations of collagen-vascular diseases not listed elsewhere (including scleroderma, calcinosis cutis, subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus, and dermatomyositis)) — evaluated under the General Rating Formula for the Skin at 0, 10, 30, or 60 percent depending on the percentage of body or exposed-area involvement and on the duration and constancy of required systemic therapy; DC 7809 (discoid lupus erythematosus) is the alternative code where the morphology is discoid rather than subacute. Qualified-human rating review required
primaryCondition: Service-connected hypertension (hypertensive vascular disease) treated with hydrochlorothiazide or a hydrochlorothiazide-containing combination product
primaryDiagnosticCode: 38 CFR § 4.104, DC 7101 (hypertensive vascular disease (hypertension and isolated systolic hypertension)): 10 percent at diastolic pressure predominantly 100 or more, or systolic predominantly 160 or more, or as the minimum evaluation for a history of diastolic pressure predominantly 100 or more requiring continuous medication for control, with Note (1) requiring confirmation by readings taken two or more times on at least three different days
etiologicalMechanism: Photosensitization and autoantibody-induction sequence: hydrochlorothiazide and its metabolites absorb ultraviolet radiation in the UVA range and, on photoactivation, generate reactive species that damage keratinocytes and alter the presentation of nuclear antigens; in genetically susceptible individuals this drives an interface dermatitis with prominent epidermal photosensitivity and induces Ro/SS-A (anti-SSA) autoantibodies directed against a ribonucleoprotein that translocates to the keratinocyte surface after ultraviolet exposure, where antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity produces the characteristic annular, polycyclic, photodistributed lesions of subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus. The reaction spares the kidneys and central nervous system in typical cases, distinguishing it clinically from systemic drug-induced lupus, and it is characteristically reversible: lesions clear within weeks of withdrawing the offending drug, and recurrence after rechallenge has been documented. Reed et al. (PMID 3873891) reported five patients taking hydrochlorothiazide who developed photosensitive eruptions with the clinical and histologic features of subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus and antibodies to the SS-A(Ro) antigen; the eruptions cleared after the drug was discontinued, anti-SS-A antibodies disappeared in one patient after thiazide withdrawal, and rechallenge with hydrochlorothiazide reproduced the dermatitis — the original human evidence, including the rechallenge that supports a causal rather than coincidental relationship. Lowe et al. (PMID 21039412) systematically reviewed drug-induced subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus, noting that the initial appearance of SCLE lesions with Ro/SS-A autoantibodies as an adverse reaction to hydrochlorothiazide was first reported in 1985, that an increasing number of drug classes has since been implicated, and that most cases resolved within weeks of drug withdrawal with Ro/SS-A autoantibodies present in about 80 percent of cases where such data were available. Callen (PMID 20693204) reviews drug-induced subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus and records that the first description dates to 1985, when a series of five patients was found to have hydrochlorothiazide-induced SCLE, and that at least 40 other drugs have since been implicated. Framing under 38 CFR § 3.310: this is a § 3.310(a) proximate-causation theory pleaded as a medication side effect, in which a disability caused by treatment of the service-connected hypertension is itself service-connected because the thiazide was prescribed for that service-connected condition. It is not a § 3.310(b) aggravation theory; aggravation would be the correct theory only where the record shows pre-existing cutaneous lupus or another photosensitive dermatosis and the claim is that the thiazide exposure measurably worsened a baseline skin disease, in which case the drug-attributable increment must be separated from the natural progression of that baseline dermatosis and § 3.310(b) governs. Chronology is decisive and the corresponding § 3.310(a) or (b) analysis requires: a prescription record identifying hydrochlorothiazide or a thiazide-containing product with start and stop dates; onset of the eruption after the drug was started, in a photodistributed pattern; dermatologic or histologic confirmation of an interface dermatitis compatible with SCLE and, where available, positive Ro/SS-A antibody testing; and documented improvement or resolution after the drug was withdrawn, since the natural history of resolution on withdrawal is itself strong evidence of the drug's causal role. Only then can an examiner state that the subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus is at least as likely as not caused by the thiazide prescribed for the service-connected hypertension — a conclusion requiring documented chronology, accounted-for competing causes, and an approximate balance of evidence consistent with § 3.102. Competing causes that must be excluded or weighed include idiopathic subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (which carries systemic associations and requires different prognostic counseling), systemic lupus erythematosus, discoid lupus, dermatomyositis, polymorphous light eruption, photosensitive drug reactions to other agents such as terbinafine, proton pump inhibitors, calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors, or tumor necrosis factor inhibitors, rosacea and seborrheic dermatitis, and tinea corporis; the fact that more than 40 drugs have been implicated means the prescriber's specific agent must be the one documented in the record. No individual probability is asserted here. No intentional rechallenge, unsupervised discontinuation of an antihypertensive, or patient-specific prescribing recommendation is made. Rating discipline under § 4.14: two or more skin conditions may be combined under § 4.25 only if separate areas of skin are involved, and where two conditions involve the same area the highest single evaluation applies, so an SCLE rating may not be pyramided with a dermatitis or scar rating for the same skin; the note to DC 7809 likewise bars combining that code with the systemic lupus code.

medicalEvidence.title: Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus associated with hydrochlorothiazide therapy
medicalEvidence.authors: B R Reed; J C Huff; S K Jones; P W Orton; L A Lee; D A Norris
medicalEvidence.summary: Report of five patients taking hydrochlorothiazide who developed photosensitive eruptions with the clinical and histologic features of subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus and antibodies to the SS-A(Ro) antigen; eruptions cleared after the drug was discontinued, anti-SS-A antibodies disappeared in one patient after thiazide withdrawal, and rechallenge reproduced the dermatitis — the founding human evidence of causal drug induction.

medicalEvidence.title: A systematic review of drug-induced subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus
medicalEvidence.authors: G C Lowe; C L Henderson; R H Grau; C B Hansen; R D Sontheimer
medicalEvidence.summary: Systematic review of the drug-induced SCLE literature reporting that the first cases were hydrochlorothiazide-induced and that the number of implicated drugs has grown, that most cases resolve spontaneously within weeks of drug withdrawal, and that Ro/SS-A autoantibodies were present in about 80 percent of cases with such data — the pooled clinical picture applied in this row.

medicalEvidence.title: Drug-induced subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus
medicalEvidence.summary: Review of drug-induced SCLE recording that the first description dates to 1985, when a series of five patients were found to have hydrochlorothiazide-induced SCLE, and that at least 40 other drugs have since been implicated in inducing SCLE — the historical and differential-diagnosis context for attributing a given eruption to a specific prescribed agent.
